title: The Death Of The Middle: How Airlines Are Splitting Into Premium & Ultra-Budget
authors: Jacob Johnson, Aaron Spray, Prachi Patel
description:
Affluent and premium leisure travelers are spending record amounts on personal space and lie-flat comfort, driving premium seat revenue up at roughly twice the rate of standard economy.
Airlines added premium economy recliners and enclosed business class suites at the front of the aircraft while introducing stripped-down basic economy fares at the back.
Full-service airlines caught wind of this, realizing that premium economy and business class generate far greater profit per square foot of floor space than standard economy rows.
In the fourth quarter of 2025, Delta reached a landmark moment when premium cabin revenue reached $5.7 billion, surpassing main cabin ticket sales of $5.62 billion for the first time.
The financial burden of premium upgrades is therefore transferred to credit card spending, establishing a self-reinforcing ecosystem for airlines where loyalty earnings continuously fuel premium cabin demand.
text:
Across the airline industry, it seems that the traditional middle tier of commercial air travel is on its way to the history books. It has always been common to see legacy carriers and low-cost airlinesalike depend on a standardized main cabin product to generate steady baseline revenue. Today, that undifferentiated middle is rapidly disappearing as commercial aviation splits into two profitable extremes: high-yield premium cabins at one end and unbundled ultra-budget fares at the other.

Executives across the industry now describe this new landscape as a barbell market. Affluent and premium leisure travelers are spending record amounts on personal space and lie-flat comfort, driving premium seat revenue up at roughly twice the rate of standard economy. At the same time, price-sensitive passengers are migrating toward absolute bottom-tier pricing. Airlines offering an average product at an average price are finding themselves caught in a financial trap without pricing power or a sustainable cost advantage.

What Happened To Standard Economy?

Main cabin seating historically served as the financial engine of commercial aviation, cross-subsidizing full-service airline operations through sheer passenger volume. Rising fuel prices, escalating crew wages, and elevated airport handling fees have completely rewritten those floor-space economics. Standard economy class tickets on their own now generate razor-thin or negative profit margins without secondary upsells, not something that any airline is willing to rely on anymore.

To protect their profit margins, legacy network carriers have begun to colonize both ends of the market. Airlines added premium economy recliners and enclosed business class suites at the front of the aircraft while introducing stripped-down basic economy fares at the back. Basic economy allowed full-service airlines to match the advertised ticket prices of budget competitors on online travel agencies and metasearch engines. Carriers now compete directly on price at the low end while offering superior international networks, eroding the price advantage that low-cost airlines spent decades building.

Middle-tier airlines have been left in a precarious position. Regional carriers and mid-market operators that lacked either luxury premium suites or a radical low-cost structure lost their ability to command premium fares. Without a loyalty ecosystem to pull high-value travelers or a low-cost structure to withstand fare wars, the middle ground became the least profitable segment in modern aviation. As three-class and four-class cabin configurations become the standard across long-haul and short-haul fleets, the era of the uniform, single-tier main cabin has come to an end.

The Numbers Prove The Change

Legacy network carriers have greatly restructured their internal economics around high-yield front cabins. The post-pandemic shift in passenger habits proved that travelers are increasingly willing to pay extra for personal space, early boarding, and superior comfort. Full-service airlines caught wind of this, realizing that premium economy and business class generate far greater profit per square foot of floor space than standard economy rows. Consequently, major airlines are now reconfiguring twin-aisle and single-aisle fleets alike, expanding premium seating footprints and shrinking traditional main cabin layouts.

Financial results across major carriers help bring this change to light. Delta Air Lines generated a record $58.3 billion in operating revenue for 2025, powered by high-margin revenue streams that accounted for 60% of total earnings. In the fourth quarter of 2025, Delta reached a landmark moment when premium cabin revenue reached $5.7 billion, surpassing main cabin ticket sales of $5.62 billion for the first time. Widebody jets configured for international long-haul routes now feature spacious premium economy seats with 38 inches (97 centimeters) to 40 inches (102 centimeters) of pitch and 19 inches (48 centimeters) of width, generating up to 33% higher profit margins per square foot than standard economy sections with 31 inches (79 centimeters) pitch.

The shift has also changed how airline revenue management departments operate on the whole. Front cabins are no longer reserved exclusively for corporate expense accounts or full-fare business travelers. Instead, premium seats are frequently filled by premium leisure travelers purchasing cash upgrades, frequent flyers redeeming loyalty points, and hybrid workers extending personal trips. The reason for this is that airlines are capturing higher yields from individual leisure travelers, preserving the bottom line against unpredictable fluctuations in corporate travel budgets, and solidifying premium seating as the dominant engine of modern airline profitability.

Creating The Sense Of Premium

The pure Ultra-Low-Cost Carrier (ULCC) business model is experiencing a severe structural crisis that threatens its long-term viability. For over two decades, ultra-budget airlines have operated under a straightforward formula: offer an unbundled bare fare that covers only transport from point A to point B, while charging separate fees for carry-on bags, seat assignments, and basic amenities. That strategy began to crumble when industry pioneer Spirit Airlines ceased operations in May 2026, illustrating the limits of relying solely on bottom-tier ticket pricing. As legacy carriers aggressively matched base fares using basic economy tickets on primary distribution channels, pure ultra-budget carriers lost the price moat that previously protected their passenger volume.

Findings from the US Government Accountability Office (GAO) highlight how the historical cost advantages enjoyed by ULCCs have systematically eroded. Early low-cost operators built their financial moats on discounted pilot labor, cheap aircraft leases, and secondary airport fee structures. The 2026 GAO report on airline competition revealed that rapid wage convergence following post-pandemic pilot union contracts, combined with rising fuel prices and airport facility fees, narrowed the cost per available seat mile (CASM) gap between legacy airlines and budget operators. Without a substantial cost advantage to offset lower passenger yields, the traditional unbundled model produces unsustainable operating margins.

To survive this margin squeeze, surviving budget carriers across North America, Europe, and Asia are rapidly moving away from pure unbundling and toward hybrid upmarket products. Operators like Frontier Airlines have introduced extra-legroom options with guaranteed empty middle seats, such as UpFront Plus, while European and Asian low-cost carriers are bundling carry-on baggage and advance seat selection into tiered fare packages. Even long-haul low-cost models, exemplified by Zipair, are incorporating full lie-flat seats to capture price-sensitive business and premium leisure demand. Through offering pseudo-premium products, low-cost carriers are attempting to extract higher revenue per seat while abandoning the unbundled bare-fare market.

The Loyalty Push

The polarization of cabin design is backed by high-margin loyalty programs and lucrative co-branded credit card agreements. Frequent flyer programs have evolved from basic mileage reward schemes into multi-billion-dollar financial engines that generate guaranteed bank revenue regardless of jet fuel prices or economic cycles. Network carriers use these programs to build emotional and financial lock-in, creating a steady stream of high-value travelers who actively prioritize flying with a single airline to earn elite status, lounge access, and upgrade certificates.

Legacy airlines also use basic economy restrictions as a tactical lever to push budget-conscious travelers into co-branded credit cards or mid-tier fares. The idea is to remove seat selection, prohibit overhead carry-on bags, and eliminate ticket flexibility on basic economy fares, resulting in a rather painful baseline experience. Holding an airline co-branded credit card serves as a workaround, offering complimentary checked bags, priority boarding, and basic fare flexibility. Consequently, price-sensitive passengers are incentivized to sign up for annual-fee credit cards, allowing legacy airlines to convert low-yielding ticket sales into steady financial payments from bank partners.

This monetization model has democratized luxury travel for non-corporate flyers, permanently altering who sits in front cabins. Card-funded airport lounge access, complimentary upgrade certificates, and milestone rewards allow leisure travelers to gain access to business class suites and premium economy recliners without corporate expense accounts. The financial burden of premium upgrades is therefore transferred to credit card spending, establishing a self-reinforcing ecosystem for airlines where loyalty earnings continuously fuel premium cabin demand.

Segmentation Before Seats Are Even Installed

The layout of passenger accommodation (LOPA) concepts across modern narrowbody and widebody fleets reflects this growing market divide. Airline engineering departments work directly with seat manufacturers and interior integrators to optimize floor-space yield down to the square inch. As carriers convert traditional single-aisle and twin-aisle cabins into multi-class configurations, shipset specifications are heavily shifting away from dense, uniform main cabin layouts toward modular, high-yield premium zones.

On widebody aircraft such as the Boeing 787 and Airbus A350, cabin reconfigurations have systematically reduced total passenger counts to prioritize high-yield cabin space. Standard economy row pitch has been compressed to 30 inches (76 centimeters) or 31 inches (79 centimeters), which reduces individual passenger space but allows airlines to reclaim critical floor area featuring 38 inches (97 centimeters) recliners and business class sections with full lie-flat suites. Single-aisle jets are undergoing similar transformations, with narrowbodies like the Airbus A321neo sacrificing four to six rows of main cabin seating to install domestic first class or long-haul lie-flat seats.

Major European and North American legacy carriers continue to retrofit existing airframes with direct-aisle-access suites, while East Asian operators are engineering hybrid layouts on low-cost platforms. Airlines worldwide are expected to follow suit, regardless of business model, and begin to completely segment the cabin to lengths never before seen in the industry.

A Future Polarized Sky

As the undifferentiated middle tier vanishes from commercial aviation, travelers face a permanent structural shift in how flight options are priced and marketed. The traditional expectation of receiving complimentary seat selection, carry-on baggage allowance, and ticket flexibility on a standard main cabin ticket has almost disappeared entirely across major carrier networks. Passengers now need to make a clear choice at the point of purchase: to accept the operational friction of stripped-down basic economy or pay a premium for extra legroom, priority boarding, and elevated cabin service.

Ancillary charges for seat assignments, carry-on luggage, and flight changes on lower-tier tickets can quickly surpass the initial price gap of a mid-tier or premium economy ticket. On the operational side, airline executives have learned that offering an unsegmented, middle-of-the-road product without the shelter of a multi-billion-dollar loyalty program or an ultra-low cost baseline is mathematically unsustainable.

The divide between high-yield luxury flying and unbundled value transport is only going to widen as carriers induct new widebody and long-range single-aisle jets into their fleets. Airline profitability is no longer ruled by simply filling seats, but by maximizing revenue per square foot across distinct cabin tiers. As carriers refine their yield management algorithms and fleet layouts, the airlines that successfully monetize both ends of the customer spectrum will dominate global aviation, while the middle ground remains permanently extinct.

text:
The Justice Department said OpenAI and one of its subsidiaries discriminated against US workers by unfairly favoring workers with temporary visa status during the hiring process.

On Tuesday, the Justice Department announced that OpenAI and Statsig, a subsidiary software development company based in Bellevue, Washington, would pay $3.2 million to settle the allegations.

"It is illegal to discriminate against U.S. workers by preferring temporary visa holders for jobs," Assistant Attorney General Harmeet K. Dhillon said in a statement. "This substantial settlement ensures that OpenAI redresses harm and changes its recruitment practices so that U.S. workers receive a fair opportunity for highly sought-after technology positions."

OpenAI said it disagreed with the DOJ's findings, but settled the matter so it could move forward with a program to support employees "requiring immigration support."

"OpenAI's mission is to ensure that AGI benefits all of humanity," an OpenAI spokesperson said in a statement. "Fulfilling that mission and maintaining America's leadership in AI requires attracting and retaining the best talent from the United States and around the world.

"While we disagree with the DOJ's findings, we reached this agreement to resolve the matter and move forward with our PERM program, which is critical for employees and candidates requiring immigration support."

The Justice Department said it found "reasonable cause" to believe that both companies made it more difficult for US workers to apply for positions they hoped to fill with foreign workers through Permanent Labor Certification, a process known as PERM.

The Trump administration has sought to crack down on companies it has said are abusing the visa system. The PERM program allows companies to sponsor temporary visa holders for permanent status, but only if they cannot find US workers for the job following a good-faith recruitment effort.

The DOJ said OpenAI and Statsig failed to take several steps critical to the PERM process, including failing to post some jobs on external sites and not advertising the positions on the radio late at night. OpenAI also required applicants for jobs it hoped to fill via PERM recruitment to mail in paper applications, even though it usually allowed electronic applications for other positions, the DOJ said.

In total, the Justice Department said, while there were fewer than 10 positions at issue across both OpenAI and Statsig, "the resolution amount reflects the harm to US workers when they are shut out of applying for lucrative technology jobs."

Of the $3.2 million settlement, OpenAI will pay $1.2 million in civil penalties. The other $2 million is being set aside to establish a fund "to compensate victims of the companies' discriminatory practices."

This story was originally published on CFO Dive. To receive daily news and insights, subscribe to our free daily CFO Dive newsletter.

Dive Brief:

Best Buy appointed retail industry veteran and former Nordstrom CFO Anne Bramman, 58, as its next finance chief, effective Aug. 19, according to a Monday press release.

The Minneapolis-based consumer technology retailer's previous long-time CFO Matt Bilunas left the company on July 31 and CEO Corie Barry has taken on the additional role of interim CFO until Bramman arrives. The company is also getting a new CEO in November when Best Buy Chief Customer, Product and Fulfillment Officer Jason Bonfig is poised to succeed Barry.

"Overall, we like this hiring," Telsey Advisory Group analysts led by Joseph Feldman said in a Tuesday note, calling her an effective and "seasoned" consumer finance executive. "It pairs incoming CEO Bonfig with a consumer and retail expert who has financial and operational experience. And, importantly, she brings fresh perspective from outside the company."

Dive Insight:

While Best Buy has seen revenue slow in recent years, incoming CEO Bonfig's vision includes expanding Best Buy's reach in a number of ways including opening more medium and small-format stores and growing through secondary business such as advertising, CFO Dive sister publication Retail Dive reported.

In its note Telsey maintained its "outperform rating" on Best Buy and raised its 12-month price target to $95 from $90. "We believe Best Buy continues to execute well and maintain/gain market share in consumer electronics, based on its ability to introduce newness, leverage its scale and vendor relationships, manage costs, and operate efficiently," the report states.

Bramman has most recently worked as a senior adviser and executive coach at Boston Consulting Group, according to her LinkedIn profile.

She peviously served as CFO of Circana, a consumer analytics company from June 2023 to August 2024. She also worked as finance chief of department store chain Nordstrom from June of 2017 to December of 2022. She was also finance chief of Avery Dennisson and Carnival Cruise Lines.

At Best Buy, Bramman's compensation will include an annual base salary of $950,000, according to a company filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission. She will also get a sign-on cash award of $500,000 and a sign-on equity award valued at $1.25 million.

"I've long admired Best Buy's ability to adapt, innovate and stay deeply connected to its customers," Bramman said in a statement in the release. "I'm thrilled to join the company and I look forward to working with Jason and the impressive Best Buy team to help accelerate growth and build an exciting future together."

name: OpenAI
title: How an OpenAI influencer trip backfired - The Verge
description:
The brand trip is a right of passage for influencers.
Many of the content creators appear to be in the career and business niches, posting about workplace culture or about being CEOs.
Typically, if an influencer is on a brand trip it’s inescapable — every little luxury, every meal, every activity is TikToked and photo dumped.
AI companies have used influencer marketing in straightforward ways, like paying creators to make content about their product offerings.
But they’ve also dabbled in the kind of influencer marketing people expert from more traditional consumer brands: Anthropic has hosted more lowkey influencer dinners at trendy locations with lifestyle influencers, and there are rumblings of a second OpenAI trip on the West Coast.
text:
The brand trip is a right of passage for influencers. It’s a mark of legitimacy that a sponsor wants to invite them on an all-expenses-paid vacation, often with luxurious freebies and activities. Trips can also spur hard feelings from uninvited influencers, trigger criticism from the public, and project a certain frivolousness.

Usually it is fast fashion companies or beauty brands flying out influencers with the goal of flooding social media with sponsored content. This time, it was a major AI company.

Over the weekend, several influencers began posting about OpenAI’s “first ever brand trip,” which appears to have taken place outside of New York City at a nature-filled retreat (for those curious, it looks to be the Instagram-bait Wildflower Farms). The trip was marketed as “Summer Club,” and influencers posted photos and videos from their cabins, showing off branded merch and monogrammed pajamas and talking vaguely about the scheduled programming. Many of the content creators appear to be in the career and business niches, posting about workplace culture or about being CEOs. Grace McCarrick, who has 145,000 followers on TikTok, vlogged from her suite as she ran a bath at night. Another influencer, Nat Lucy (57,000 followers), filmed herself spotting a deer outside of her cabin. All hell broke loose.

“People will literally sell their soul and their planet down the river for a nice free hotel room,” one commenter on TikTok wrote under McCarrick’s video. “Wow! Beautiful greenery! They should put a data center there!” reads a comment on Lucy’s post. Most of the videos got relatively little traction: McCarrick’s video has just under 300 likes, and Lucy’s video has fewer than 15,000 views. It’s measly engagement compared to what other splashy brand trips can command — but videos reacting to the trip have made it something of a scandal (a pair of clips alone has over half a million combined views).

Many of the comments on the influencers’ videos cite the environmental effects of the AI boom, the contentious buildout of data centers across the US, and the potential for job replacement or job loss as a result of companies integrating AI in the workplace. Some also questioned why so many of the content creators who went on the trip appeared to be young women, as if OpenAI was targeting a specific demographic via media they were more connected to (though based on photos and videos posted to social media, there were men on the trip, too). According to Pew, even as the AI usage gap between men and women has all but disappeared, women tend to view AI more negatively and are twice as likely to say AI will negatively impact them personally. Some audiences wondered whether female influencers were essentially being used to launder the reputation of an industry under scrutiny.

McCarrick, who describes herself as a creator who talks about “soft skills we need at work to millions online and to teams like Spotify, Amazon, Uber and DoorDash,” has since made multiple videos responding to commenters accusing her of essentially abandoning her morals for a fancy trip. On LinkedIn she wrote that she “genuinely had no idea that people were this anti-AI,” and that the negative response to her videos exposed her to “the shocking AI psychosis running rampant online” — by which she means anger about AI, not the more common definition of being driven to paranoia or delusions of grandeur by using AI. People in the real world “do not run around like a chicken with their heads cut off, screaming about water usage and wildlife and (curiously) fascism,” she wrote.

None of the influencers The Verge reached out to responded to requests for comment. OpenAI said creator marketing is part of how they reach people and that the event was meant to be educational.

“Creators are an important part of our community and how people get information and learn about our products today,” OpenAI spokesperson Edie Campbell-Urban said in an email. “We welcome healthy debate as AI becomes more prevalent, and we value creators who choose to engage with us, attend our events, ask tough questions, and learn alongside everyone else. We’ll continue to value them, just as we do traditional media and other marketing partners.”

Setting aside the backlash to the trip for a moment, a few things stand out. First, all things considered, this appears to be a relatively simple trip. That’s not to say it wasn’t luxurious — the rooms at the retreat cost upwards of $2,000 a night — but it is nothing compared to the brands that go all out in order to milk content from every last moment (some commenters poked fun at the fact that it was a domestic trip, not a far-flung, international vacation). Second, there’s a sense that everyone involved is testing the waters: Multiple influencers noted it was the first brand trip they’d attended, and one influencer indicated they were not paid for their attendance, which big brands often do for top talent. Third and most interestingly, the goals of the trip are muddled: It’s not entirely clear what the influencers were actually doing on the trip, because there is surprisingly little content online from the event. Typically, if an influencer is on a brand trip it’s inescapable — every little luxury, every meal, every activity is TikToked and photo dumped. Instead of content about the capabilities of ChatGPT, the videos and photos are largely aspirational lifestyle content focused on the free swag and pretty setting — and even then, there’s a conspicuous lack of content, period. There isn’t the same flood of picturesque montages, clips from expert sessions or Q&As, or summaries of what a creator learned from their time with OpenAI. At least not yet.

AI companies have used influencer marketing in straightforward ways, like paying creators to make content about their product offerings. But they’ve also dabbled in the kind of influencer marketing people expert from more traditional consumer brands: Anthropic has hosted more lowkey influencer dinners at trendy locations with lifestyle influencers, and there are rumblings of a second OpenAI trip on the West Coast.

As backlash to the industry has grown, AI companies have adjusted how they communicate with the public: “Your jobs will soon be obsolete” has clearly not been the right framing for why people should trust these companies or get on board with their mission. Instead, AI companies like OpenAI and Anthropic have tried to add a bit of human touch, whether that’s through in-person pop-up coffee shops, stylized merch drops, or ad campaigns that take concerns people have about AI and try to turn them into pro-AI inspirational content.

What better way to reach consumers directly than through the talking heads they already know and trust? Influencers are a convenient vessel, both for brands looking to disseminate their message and for the inevitable backlash from audiences who give them a platform in the first place. In this case, the content broke containment out of the girlboss-style business circles into the mainstream — an AI brand trip dressed up as an aspirational lifestyle retreat is both confusing and enraging to a public fatigued by this line of work. By tapping a certain kind of creator for a weekend of sponsored content, OpenAI is able to test a new audience without fully committing; it’s the content creators, after all, who will get the angry comments, whose faces will be plastered on the backgrounds of an ever-increasing number of reaction videos (influencers received similar backlash for a Shein brand trip in 2023). The AI industry wants the soft power and cultural relevance influencers wield and realized the price of reaching their audience is surprisingly cheap. You get what you pay for.

text:
Uber Technologies (UBER +0.74%) is an intriguing stock for a number of reasons, including strong core business and user growth, strong adjusted earnings and cash flow, and significant value returned to shareholders through share buybacks.

Perhaps most intriguing is that it plans to avoid heavy capital investment to develop and manufacture self-driving vehicles by partnering with companies such as Waymo, which is owned by Alphabet (GOOG +0.94%) (GOOGL +1.36%), as well as with Baidu and Nvidia. But if Waymo's recent announcement is any indication, Uber's future might be competing against former self-driving car partners.

What's going on?

In the latest development between Uber and Waymo, the latter is exploring options to exit its robotaxi partnership with the former. Currently, Uber offers rides in autonomous Waymo vehicles exclusively in Austin and Atlanta. Waymo gave Uber notice that it plans to launch its own service app in those two cities at the beginning of 2028.

Waymo will run its service alongside its existing business with Uber and will keep its fleet of vehicles on Uber's platform through May 2028, when the current contract ends. "We believe in a vibrant and collaborative AV ecosystem that champions innovation and provides riders with a choice in how they experience this technology," said a Waymo spokesperson, according to Automotive News. "This is essential to the industry's future and to our vision of making the Waymo app and the safety of our technology available to riders everywhere."

Hospitality Network Expands Across Europe

Beyond its owned locations, Wojo provides access to hundreds of partner workspaces, many located within Accor hotels across France and other European destinations.

The acquisition broadens IWG’s hospitality-focused workspace offering and expands its reach across Europe, giving customers access to both companies’ networks.

The transaction follows IWG’s acquisition of German flexible workspace operator Design Offices earlier this year, reflecting the company’s strategy of expanding through acquisitions alongside organic growth.

Microsoft plans to bring Xbox 360 games to PC from 2027

Microsoft is preparing to bring Xbox 360 games to PC, handhelds and its next-generation Xbox hardware. The program will reportedly begin rolling out between 2027 and 2028.

The details come from a Microsoft document sent to game developers and reviewed by The Verge. We already covered the leaked roadmap, but the new report confirms that the Xbox 360 catalog is part of Microsoft’s broader backward compatibility plan.

Publishers will control pricing and Game Pass access

What’s new in The Verge’s report is that Xbox 360 games will run on the next-generation Project Helix console, Xbox-branded PCs and handheld devices. Publishers will need to opt their games into the program. Microsoft will handle engineering, certification and support. Publishers will retain control over licensing, pricing and whether each game appears on Xbox Game Pass.

The rollout is described as gradual, suggesting that only part of the Xbox 360 catalog will become available at first. The document does not identify which games or publishers have joined the program.

Microsoft is also planning a full launch of original Xbox games on PC in October 2026. The first phase announced in July included four games, with more titles expected once publishers approve their catalogs.

One more thing to read from this roadmap is that the next-gen Xbox is confirmed for 2027.

title: Microsoft's $100B Azure Year Shows Enterprise AI Is Moving Beyond One Model
description:
For the full fiscal year, Microsoft revenue reached $331.8 billion, up 18%, while operating income reached $155.2 billion, up 21%.
It is arguing that enterprise AI will depend on model choice, governed data, context, agent controls, developer platforms, and business applications working together.
AI strategy is moving away from single-model bets and toward model portfolios selected by quality, latency, cost, compliance, and business continuity.
Dynamics, GitHub Show Where AI Turns into Workflow Microsoft’s business applications story is also becoming more agentic.
The implication is that Microsoft’s AI business model is moving beyond seats alone.
text:
Microsoft closed fiscal 2026 with Azure surpassing $100 billion in annual revenue for the first time.

Microsoft announced on July 29 that Q4 revenue reached $90.0 billion, up 18% year over year, while operating income reached $40.6 billion, also up 18%. Net income was $35.8 billion, up 31% on a GAAP basis, and diluted earnings per share was $4.81, up 32% on a GAAP basis.

For the full fiscal year, Microsoft revenue reached $331.8 billion, up 18%, while operating income reached $155.2 billion, up 21%. Microsoft Cloud revenue was $59.3 billion in Q4, up 27%, and commercial remaining performance obligation increased 84% to $678 billion.

Satya Nadella, chairman and CEO of Microsoft, said Azure revenue surpassed $100 billion for the first time and Microsoft 365 Copilot reached more than 30 million paid seats. He said those milestones reflect customer confidence in Microsoft’s role powering AI transformation.

The quarter gives Microsoft a stronger proof point for its AI platform strategy. The company is not only selling cloud capacity. It is arguing that enterprise AI will depend on model choice, governed data, context, agent controls, developer platforms, and business applications working together.

Multi-Model AI Becomes the Cloud Battleground

On Microsoft’s earnings call, Nadella said the company now offers more than 11,000 models across Azure, including models from OpenAI, Anthropic, Mistral, xAI, and Microsoft’s own MAI family. He also said Microsoft has seen a fivefold increase since the start of the year in customers building with models from multiple providers.

That is a critical signal for enterprise software buyers. AI strategy is moving away from single-model bets and toward model portfolios selected by quality, latency, cost, compliance, and business continuity. Nadella said Microsoft is building a system where the harness, context, memory, and action space are separated from any one model family, making models substitutable.

For ERP leaders, that architecture matters because business applications will increasingly use different models for different tasks. A finance agent, customer-service agent, developer assistant, sales workflow, or supply-chain process may not need the same model. The platform question becomes where those models are governed, how they access enterprise data, and how agent actions are controlled.

Microsoft pointed to Levi Strauss & Co. as an example, saying the company is using OpenAI and Anthropic models on Foundry as it brings more than 1,000 domain-specific agents into a unified enterprise AI platform.

Dynamics, GitHub Show Where AI Turns into Workflow

Microsoft’s business applications story is also becoming more agentic. Dynamics 365 revenue increased 13% in Q4, or 12% in constant currency, while Nadella said Microsoft is exposing more than 650,000 MCP actions across sales, finance, supply chain, HR, and customer service.

Those actions allow agents to access business context and take action using the same data models, rules, permissions, security guardrails, and audit trails as application users.

That reinforces Microsoft’s broader MCP strategy. The company is turning Model Context Protocol into a connection layer between agents and business systems, including ERP and CRM workflows. For customers, the promise is that agents can act inside governed application structures rather than operate as disconnected automations.

GitHub adds another dimension to the story. Nadella said GitHub Copilot now has 50 million users and that GitHub has 225 million users overall, with more than 90% of the Fortune 500 using the platform for AI-powered development. He also said Copilot revenue accelerated more than 60% quarter over quarter after Microsoft introduced usage-based billing.

The implication is that Microsoft’s AI business model is moving beyond seats alone. Microsoft is layering consumption-based economics into Copilot, Cowork, Dynamics 365, GitHub Copilot, and future agentic offerings, tying revenue more closely to usage and outcomes.

What This Means for ERP Insiders

Enterprise AI is becoming multi-model by default. Microsoft’s 11,000-model catalog and fivefold increase in multi-provider customers show that buyers want flexibility across model families, cost profiles, latency needs, and compliance constraints. For ERP architects and AI platform teams, the next design priority is deciding how model choice will be governed across finance, supply chain, HR, sales, service, and development workflows.

Agentic ERP will depend on governed actions, not just smarter answers. Microsoft’s Dynamics 365 MCP actions show how agents are being connected to business context, permissions, audit trails, and application rules. For CIOs, CFOs, and process owners, the practical test is whether agents can execute work inside existing controls rather than create a new layer of untracked automation.

text:
The Linux Foundation’s Tokenomics Foundation—focused on standardizing how companies measure and manage AI token costs and connect them to business value—officially launches today, backed by about 30 initial members. Founding supporters at the time of launch include companies such as Accenture, Booking.com, BNY, Flexera, IBM, JPMorgan Chase, KPMG, Oracle, SAP, and ServiceNow.

That roster reflects the foundation’s goal of uniting “token users and suppliers”—companies burning through tokens and the model providers and cloud platforms selling access to them—under one vendor-neutral roof.

To learn more, I asked J.R. Storment, executive director of the Tokenomics Foundation, a few questions:

CFO Daily: How should a CFO who has never budgeted for token consumption start building that competency?

Storment: A CFO should collaborate with their teams to build visibility into consumption by model, workload, team, and project. The goal is to guide budgets toward outcomes rather than flat limits: a flat limit tells you nothing about whether the spend earned anything, while an AI budget tied to value survives a rising bill.

CFOs should partner with the CTO, CIO, and CAIO on what AI activity the business runs today, what is planned, and what each is expected to produce. The CFO does not need the deep AI vocabulary, they need a counterpart who has it and a forward view rather than retroactive.

Credit pricing, seat licenses, and bundled “unlimited AI” plans sever usage from cost, and you cannot allocate costs you cannot measure to understand value. Managing how contracts expose token-level telemetry takes no new literacy, but gains you more visibility into AI value.

CFO Daily: What specific gap in the market made the Linux Foundation decide that a standalone Tokenomics Foundation was needed, rather than folding this work entirely into the existing FinOps Foundation?

Storment: The Tokenomics Foundation arrives at a defining moment for the global technology economy when every company in the world is struggling to quantify the value of AI. While per-token costs fell heavily during 2023-2025 they have leveled off—and new model token prices are rising—making AI costs the largest and fastest-growing line item on enterprise technology budgets. Add to that the pace of AI change, the increasing cardinality of model options, the rapidly rising costs with projects going into production leading to AI value questions. This has made tokenomics a CEO-level concern and organizations are looking for alignment on industry best practices and standards for AI ROI.

There will be close alignment with the FinOps Foundation, however tokenomics and the AI supply chain is broader and deeper, it also has different technical challenges that require dedicated focused investment and governing strategy.

CFO Daily: With founding members spanning hyperscalers, enterprises, and vendors, some of them are competitors. How did you get them to work together? How do you keep the framework from tilting toward suppliers’ interests over buyers’ cost-management needs?

Storment: The Linux Foundation has a deep history of bringing organizations together in a vendor-neutral environment. We focus first on the needs of the end-user enterprises and aim to solve their challenges in a collaborative environment. Organizations want to standardize pre-competitive technology, frameworks, and benchmarks to avoid the duplicative work for everyone so they can focus on their unique offerings. This also adds additional value to end users who can then accelerate investment and get more value from their AI as more pieces are standardized.

Best practice development includes input from a global technology value community of more than 120,000 people. The outputs of the Tokenomics Foundation will always be focused on vendor-agnostic best practices to solve the tokenomics challenge.

CFO Daily: The governing board convened on July 30, and the technical steering committee is forming next. Do you have a timeline for when there will be usable frameworks or benchmarks created?

Storment: Things are moving very quickly in the world of tokenomics, so it’s a balance between speed and standardization. We’ve already begun to publish lightweight best practices such as the Big-T Notation framework, with more projects in draft for presentation at the upcoming Tokenomicon in Amsterdam in September.

title: Kroger Announces Store Closures as Retail Giant Resets Following Failed Albertsons Merger
description:
While the closures represent only a small fraction of Kroger’s nationwide estate of nearly 2,800 stores, they signal a broader strategic shift.
Industry analysts say the planned closures reflect a wider trend sweeping through the supermarket industry.
Rather than measuring success by the number of stores operated, supermarket companies are focusing on productivity, technology, customer experience and profitability.
Modern grocery retail is becoming less about size and more about efficiency.
For Kroger, the restructuring marks the beginning of a new chapter following the disappointment of the failed Albertsons merger.
text:
By ISN Magazine

Less than a year after the collapse of its proposed merger with Albertsons, Kroger has unveiled plans to close approximately 60 underperforming supermarkets across the United States, marking the beginning of a significant restructuring programme designed to strengthen the company’s long-term competitiveness.

The decision has become one of the biggest stories in the U.S. grocery industry, highlighting the challenges facing traditional supermarket operators as they navigate changing consumer behaviour, rising operating costs and fierce competition from Walmart, Costco, Aldi and Amazon.

While the closures represent only a small fraction of Kroger’s nationwide estate of nearly 2,800 stores, they signal a broader strategic shift. Rather than pursuing expansion for expansion’s sake, the retailer is concentrating investment on stores and markets with the strongest growth potential.

The announcement follows one of the most turbulent periods in Kroger’s history.

The company’s ambitious $24.6 billion acquisition of Albertsons was blocked after months of legal challenges from federal and state regulators, who argued that the merger would reduce competition and potentially lead to higher grocery prices for American consumers.

When the deal collapsed, Kroger was forced to reassess its long-term business strategy.

Instead of focusing on integrating thousands of additional supermarkets, management is now concentrating on improving operational efficiency, modernising existing stores and strengthening digital capabilities.

Industry analysts say the planned closures reflect a wider trend sweeping through the supermarket industry.

Retailers are increasingly evaluating store performance using advanced data analytics rather than relying solely on geographic coverage. Factors including customer traffic, profitability, online order volumes, local competition and demographic trends now play a central role in determining whether a supermarket remains viable.

At the same time, supermarkets are investing billions of dollars in technology.

Artificial intelligence is improving inventory forecasting, automated distribution centres are reducing supply chain costs, and digital loyalty programmes are helping retailers better understand customer purchasing habits.

Rather than maintaining underperforming locations, many retailers are redirecting capital towards technology, store refurbishment and e-commerce infrastructure.

For employees and local communities, however, store closures inevitably create uncertainty.

Kroger has stated that it intends to transfer as many affected employees as possible to nearby locations, minimising job losses while maintaining customer service in surrounding markets.

The company also emphasises that the restructuring is intended to create a stronger and more sustainable business rather than simply reducing costs.

Competition within the U.S. grocery sector has never been more intense.

Walmart continues to dominate food retail through scale and pricing, Costco remains highly successful with its membership model, Aldi is rapidly expanding across America, and Amazon continues to develop its grocery operations through Whole Foods Market and online delivery services.

Against this backdrop, every investment decision has become increasingly important.

Retail experts believe the closure programme represents a shift in thinking across the industry.

Rather than measuring success by the number of stores operated, supermarket companies are focusing on productivity, technology, customer experience and profitability. Modern grocery retail is becoming less about size and more about efficiency.

For Kroger, the restructuring marks the beginning of a new chapter following the disappointment of the failed Albertsons merger.

The company remains one of America’s largest food retailers, but its future growth will now depend on organic expansion, digital innovation and operational excellence rather than large-scale acquisitions.

As the grocery industry continues to evolve, Kroger’s latest move illustrates a simple reality: in today’s retail environment, success is no longer determined by having the most stores—it is determined by having the right stores.

Ex-Uber founder and CEO Travis Kalanick is back in the ride-hail business — but this time in the skies.

Air taxi maker Joby Aviation (JOBY) on Monday announced a strategic partnership with Atoms, the industrial AI and infrastructure company founded by Kalanick, to acquire and develop a network of "vertiports," or heliports for air taxis, across the US as Joby nears its commercial service launch.

The partnership will initially target Florida, New York, and Texas, where Joby is preparing to launch early operations under the White House-backed eVTOL Integration Pilot Program (eIPP), as well as California.

Joby stock rose on the news.

Atoms Real Estate will design and build the sites as "multimodal transportation hubs" where electric aircraft, autonomous ground vehicles, and ridesharing converge, anchored by on-site power for charging and operations.

For Kalanick, a pioneer in the logistics and demand-matching space, the deal made sense.

"Smart cities require innovative real estate and infrastructure development," Kalanick, who co-founded Uber (UBER) and led the ride-hailing giant until his 2017 ouster, said in a statement. "As new transport modes and smart city services become available, designing and deploying a new asset class to support them is critical."

Joby founder and CEO JoeBen Bevirt called Atoms "a natural partner," given its vision for "ambitious infrastructure projects that combine technology, operations, and customer experience."

The deal brings Kalanick back to an industry he transformed. After leaving Uber, he built Atoms into a holding company spanning food, mining, and transportation, with businesses including CloudKitchens, Otter, Picnic, Lab37, ProFood, and Pronto.

Signing a deal for land-based operations is the next step for Joby. The company flew its first FAA-conforming aircraft and entered the final stage of FAA type certification, with piloted flights in the San Francisco Bay Area and New York City.

Last month, the company finalized a deal with Virgin Atlantic to bring air taxi service to the UK, with Virgin serving as its exclusive airline partner there.

Joby also counts Delta Air Lines (DAL) as a partner and investor, as well as Toyota (TM) for manufacturing, and Kalanick's former company Uber for integrating air taxis on Uber's platform.

name: Michelin
title: Michelin Says India Tyre Manufacturing Is About Market Access, Not Lower Costs
description:
Michelin India Managing Director Shantanu Deshpande said the Primacy 5 has been priced according to its safety, comfort, life and efficiency proposition, rather than its country of manufacture.
₹3,400 Crore Chennai Commitment Michelin invested ₹686 crore, or €76 million, in its passenger car tyre line in September 2025.
The French company began passenger car tyre production in India with the Primacy 5, a premium tyre developed for sedans and SUVs and compatible with internal combustion engine, hybrid and electric vehicles.
The company’s Chennai plant has a combined capacity of around 54,000 tonnes for truck, bus and passenger car tyres.
The domestic market will also remain the priority for passenger car tyre production.
text:
Michelin’s decision to manufacture passenger car tyres in India is aimed at moving closer to a growing premium-vehicle market and adapting its products to local conditions, rather than securing an immediate cost advantage, a senior company executive said.

“The reason for us to produce it is not a cost reason,” Vitor Silva, president of Michelin’s Africa, India and Middle East region, said during a media interaction.

Production at the company’s new passenger car tyre line in Chennai will initially cost more than at some of its established overseas factories because Michelin must depreciate the fresh investment, Silva said. The company expects costs to become comparable with its plants in Asia and Eastern Europe as production scales up.

“At the beginning of a project, the tyre will always be a little bit more expensive because we have all the investments that we need to depreciate,” he said.

However, the higher initial manufacturing cost will not automatically translate into a higher retail price.

Michelin India Managing Director Shantanu Deshpande said the Primacy 5 has been priced according to its safety, comfort, life and efficiency proposition, rather than its country of manufacture.

“We are not going to increase or decrease the price of our Primacy 5 just because it is made in India or because it is being made in a new factory,” Deshpande said.

₹3,400 Crore Chennai Commitment

Michelin invested ₹686 crore, or €76 million, in its passenger car tyre line in September 2025. This was in addition to the more than ₹2,800 crore committed to its Chennai manufacturing project in 2009.

The French company began passenger car tyre production in India with the Primacy 5, a premium tyre developed for sedans and SUVs and compatible with internal combustion engine, hybrid and electric vehicles. The tyre will be available in sizes ranging from 16 to 22 inches, with prices starting at about ₹10,000, depending on the size.

The company’s Chennai plant has a combined capacity of around 54,000 tonnes for truck, bus and passenger car tyres. Michelin plans to add products such as the Pilot Sport 5, LTX Trail and others as the operation ramps up through the end of 2027.

Further capacity additions will be made in phases based on market demand.

Bigger Vehicles Drive Localisation

Michelin’s local production push comes as Indian buyers shift towards SUVs and larger vehicles, creating greater demand for premium tyres of 16 inches and above.

The company plans to manufacture passenger car tyres ranging from 16 to 22 inches in Chennai and has said it wants to build a leadership position in the 18-inch-and-above category.

According to the Society of Indian Automobile Manufacturers, utility vehicles accounted for about 68% of domestic passenger vehicle sales in the first quarter of FY27. Their sales increased 28.6% year on year, helping overall passenger vehicle sales rise 25.9% to 1.27 million units.

Improved highways, longer leisure journeys and higher average speeds are also prompting customers to seek better braking, comfort and durability, Michelin said.

Adapted to Indian Roads

Michelin said the locally manufactured Primacy 5 follows the same core quality and performance standards as products made at its other plants.

However, the company has added material to strengthen the tyre against road hazards in India. The additional reinforcement, including more material in the sidewall, makes the Indian version slightly heavier.

The tyre has also been fine-tuned for local temperature, humidity and road conditions. “One of the advantages of having a local-to-local approach is that you can fine-tune the product to local conditions,” Silva said.

Michelin said the Chennai plant uses the same basic compounds, machinery and quality processes followed by its facilities in other markets.

Replacement Market First

Michelin will initially focus on the passenger vehicle replacement market. It expects supplies to automakers to follow as production and volumes grow.

“We will start and focus on getting our share together in the replacement market,” Deshpande said. “As we grow and as we have opportunities, the OEM segment will also happen.”

The company had followed a similar strategy in truck and bus tyres, beginning with replacement demand before supplying vehicle manufacturers.

The domestic market will also remain the priority for passenger car tyre production. Exports could follow after the Chennai line scales up. “Our priority is the local market. And then from here we can export,” Silva said.

The Middle East and Africa would be the first export destinations under Michelin’s regional manufacturing strategy. The company already exports truck tyres produced in Chennai to North America, Europe, Africa and the Middle East.

For Michelin, the immediate benefit of making passenger car tyres in India lies in gaining closer access to customers, adapting products to local use and improving availability, not in achieving a quick reduction in manufacturing costs.

title: The NFL's previous push into Europe lost $400 million. Why it's trying again | Fortune
description:

Despite its global popularity, soccer has struggled to find the same fandom in the U.S. as it boasts across Europe.
That stuff is inspirational.” This is not the first time the NFL has sought to break into Europe.
The first attempt, a 1974 plan for an Intercontinental Football League, with teams penciled in for Istanbul, Rome, Munich, West Berlin, Vienna, and Barcelona, folded before playing a single down.
In 2019, the Tottenham Hotspur Stadium in London became the first arena outside North America specifically built to accommodate an American football game.
text:
The series is part of the NFL’s strategy to deepen its foothold in Europe. “We’re using the game as a catalyst,” Tim Ellis, the league’s chief marketing officer, tells Fortune. “To get people interested, to get them talking, to get the media to pay attention.” For Ellis, the 80,000 tickets available for the Stade de France game matter far less than the millions of fans the league hopes to convert in the weeks and months after the final whistle.

There are signs the league is generating real demand overseas. London will have hosted 45 games by the end of this season and remains the league’s most mature overseas market. Melbourne and Paris, where Ellis says the league’s fan base has grown past 14 million, are also expected to draw big crowds. Ticket interest for the NFL’s Melbourne match has surpassed the Melbourne Cricket Ground’s 100,000-seat capacity, with more than 151,000 fans registering interest. Meanwhile, more than 600,000 people joined the virtual queue for last year’s Steelers game at Croke Park in Dublin. Ticket and hospitality revenue, Ellis says, pales in comparison to what the NFL hopes to build in media rights, sponsorship, and merchandise deals, once European audiences are converted into fans who watch 50-plus games a year rather than one.

The NFL isn’t the only organization running this experiment. Earlier this summer, FIFA was in the process of successfully exporting soccer to the U.S. as it joined Mexico and Canada in cohosting the World Cup. Despite its global popularity, soccer has struggled to find the same fandom in the U.S. as it boasts across Europe. Roughly a quarter (27%) of U.S. sports fans show an interest in soccer, compared with a global average of 40%, according to Sports Innovation Lab and JvM Sports. However, this World Cup has been a turning point. More than 6.25 million people attended matches through to the conclusion of the last round of 16, according to FIFA, and 18 million tuned in for the U.S. Men’s National Team opener against Paraguay across Fox’s platforms. The NFL is taking notes. “I’ve long admired FIFA for their global reach,” Ellis says, pointing to the power of “border-crossing stars” such as Lionel Messi. “Another lesson is storytelling,” he adds. “People want to know the backstories of the athletes. That stuff is inspirational.”

This is not the first time the NFL has sought to break into Europe. The first attempt, a 1974 plan for an Intercontinental Football League, with teams penciled in for Istanbul, Rome, Munich, West Berlin, Vienna, and Barcelona, folded before playing a single down. The NFL World League, established in 1989, enjoyed slightly more success.

The transatlantic tournament featured 10 teams: six from the U.S., one from Canada, and three from Europe. The league kicked off in 1991 at the Waldstadion in Germany, as the Frankfurt Galaxy took on the London Monarchs. However, the league suspended operations after its second season. Rebuilt as an all-European circuit in 1995 and rebranded NFL Europa, it limped on with squads in England, Germany, the Netherlands, Scotland, and Spain until the league finally pulled the plug in 2007.

NFL Europa never landed a TV contract in its own markets, starving it of revenue that might have kept it afloat. The venture ran up roughly $400 million in losses over 16 years, according to analysis by Chang Wan Woo, published in the Journal of Communications Studies. The constant rebranding, franchise relocations, and lack of experienced players limited the competition’s popularity, with fans showing little appetite for a developmental league playing what was considered a watered-down version of the sport.

Earlier expansion efforts struggled in part because the league assumed the product would sell itself, Ellis says: “It understood almost nothing about how outsiders actually saw the game.” To the uninitiated European viewer, American football can seem “chaotic,” he says. “[They view it] as a spectacle more than a sport: big men in gladiatorial armor colliding, stopping, colliding again, then cutting to commercials.” By contrast, 41% of Americans say football is their favorite sport, a Gallup survey found. “Most Americans absorbed the rules by cultural osmosis long before they could articulate them,” says Ellis. “Strip away that lifetime of exposure, and you’re left with, quite frankly, a baffling and barbaric game.”

Increasing the NFL’s popularity abroad has been “an incredible challenge,” Ellis says, but he believes his experience of working in the U.S. and across Europe makes him uniquely well suited to finally bridge the divide. Earlier in his career, Ellis traveled to Paris to study French. He then spent five years working his way around the world: driving tractors on a kibbutz in Israel; building platforms for North Sea oil rigs in Norway; bartending on a luxury cruise line; and briefly modeling in Tokyo. He spent 12 years in Sweden, much of it running international accounts at the advertising agency Forsman & Bodenfors, before moving client-side at Volvo. After a stint at Volkswagen, Ellis spent seven years working in Santa Monica for the video game company Activision. “After living and working all over the world, I’ve learned that markets don’t reject the product, they reject the translation,” Ellis says.

When Ellis joined the NFL in 2018, he commissioned research across the league’s priority markets to get a better understanding of the awareness and perception of the sport internationally. “Many international viewers simply hadn’t registered that these enormous men are also elite athletes, world-class sprinters, some of them Olympic medalists,” Ellis says. “They’re like ballet dancers, but they’re 280 pounds of muscle.” His team ran a parallel study: What does someone need to know to enjoy the game? The research found that the two factors most likely to put a newcomer off—the sport’s complexity and its violence—are precisely what hooks them once they develop a deeper understanding of the sport.

This information has informed the NFL’s European marketing strategy as it aims to turn casual viewers into committed ones. “The idea is not to dumb the game down,” Ellis says, “but to escort newcomers across the threshold from confusion to fascination.” The strategy is gaining traction. In 2019, the Tottenham Hotspur Stadium in London became the first arena outside North America specifically built to accommodate an American football game. Two NFL games are scheduled to be played there in October, with another being hosted at Wembley, and a fourth in Madrid.

One of the core elements of the strategy has been to give people an established U.S. club to root for and players to love, Ellis explains. All 32 NFL teams now hold designated international marketing territories, which has allowed the sport to tap into some of the tribal fandom that soccer teams enjoy across Europe. Additionally, the league is developing digital content centered on athletes’ families and backstories. This “helmets-off” strategy is designed to help international audiences get to know players and turn the sport’s stars into recognizable personalities in Europe.

The NFL has also had to rethink how to market itself to a continent that “doesn’t do swagger,” as Ellis puts it. “U.S. sports marketing runs on swagger,” he says. But the league’s own research found that what reads as charisma in Dallas can land as arrogance in Düsseldorf. “Something that we would see as confident, they would see as bro-y or too macho,” he adds. As the NFL expands overseas, it is also having to contend with anti-American sentiment in some markets. Because American football is closely woven into U.S. culture, the sport is often associated with overt displays of patriotism, such as flag ceremonies and military flyovers. Abroad, Ellis says, the league has to tread carefully, because that same patriotism can be read as “political in nature” by international audiences if it isn’t handled correctly.

Another element of the strategy involves increasing participation in the sport abroad. The NFL Academy, an elite development initiative for student athletes, is based in Loughborough, England, and has partnerships with Loughborough College and Loughborough University. The program combines academic study with daily training, giving aspiring young athletes in the U.K. an opportunity to make it professionally. “College football rosters used to be almost entirely American,” Ellis says. However, this year he expects over 30 international players to join NCAA Division I programs—the highest level of college football in the U.S. The International Player Pathway, a separate initiative established in 2017, is tasked with identifying elite global talent and developing them into NFL-ready players.

A noncontact version of the game, called flag football, has also become a fast-growing entry point for girls in the U.S. and abroad. The NFL lobbied for flag football to become an Olympic sport, and it is set to debut at the Los Angeles Games in 2028. Ellis says the NFL is already pushing to keep the noncontact variant on the program for Brisbane 2032. “We’re trying to get more Europeans to play football, not just watch it,” he says. “A child who plays the game is dramatically more likely to become a lifelong fan.”

The financial stakes explain why Europe matters so much to the league. NFL revenue topped $23 billion in the past fiscal year, according to S&P Global Market Intelligence, and the league is targeting $25 billion by 2027. Media rights are the largest contributor: The NFL’s current broadcast deal, worth nearly $110 billion over 11 years, accounts for almost half of total annual earnings. Replicating this model in Europe would represent a major financial boon. The lesson from prior endeavors is that new markets aren’t won by adapting a product to suit local tastes. They’re won, as Ellis says, “by exporting the real thing, unchanged, and building the story, stars, and trust.”

This article appears in the August/September 2026: Europe issue of Fortune with the headline “Can the NFL finally conquer Europe?”

title: Wheels Up losses continue in Q2 2026 despite improved reliability
description:
However, the Delta Air Lines-backed private jet company’s path to profitability was slowed by higher costs and slower sales attributed to its ongoing transition.
Net Loss was $107.2 million, Adjusted EBITDA loss was $26.2 million, and Adjusted EBITDAR loss was $19.9 million, although the latter two metrics showed year-over-year improvement.

READ: What Delta’s Q2 filings say about Wheels Up Q2 2026 Financials Second quarter GAAP revenues for 2026 were $182.0 million, down 4.0% year-over-year.

text:
The second-quarter results for 2026 showed Wheels Up ahead of schedule on many of its strategic initiatives, including improving operational reliability, on-time performance, fleet renewal, and cost-cutting.

However, the Delta Air Lines-backed private jet company’s path to profitability was slowed by higher costs and slower sales attributed to its ongoing transition.

GAAP revenue dropped 4% year-over-year to $182.0 million.

Net Loss was $107.2 million, Adjusted EBITDA loss was $26.2 million, and Adjusted EBITDAR loss was $19.9 million, although the latter two metrics showed year-over-year improvement.

(A chart tracking the last six quarters of Wheels Up’s financials is below.)

On the bright side, the quarter saw the number of its Signature and Custom Enterprise Solutions members grow to over 1,200, representing over 50% of programmatic members.

Signature was launched last September, although Wheels Up continued selling its legacy membership until the end of March.

Improved Operations

Completion Rate for the quarter was 99.4%, up nearly two points year over year.

On-Time Performance, defined as arriving within 30 minutes of the scheduled time, was 86.8%, up by more than six points year over year.

Through the end of July 2026, there were 119 Brand Days, dates with no cancellations, more than all of last year.

Brand Days in the most recent quarter surged to 57 from 14 in 2025.

Wheels Up On-Time Rate, Reliability Metrics

Wheels Up is the only leading private jet operator to report on-time performance and completion rate.

However, replacing its aging private jets and King Air 350 turboprop fleet 18 months ahead of plan impacted the bottom line, according to the company.

Currently, the new fleet features 28 Embraer light jets and 10 Bombardier super-midsize aircraft, according to the latest FAA Part 135 report.

Gogo’s next-generation Galileo HDX high-speed Wi-Fi has already been installed across the fleet, CEO George Mattson tells Private Jet Card Comparisons.

“I know other folks are talking about having (upgraded Wi-Fi) done in the next year and a half or so, but we’re done. Every Wheels Up plane you get on now has satellite Wi-Fi,” Mattson said.

The move to premium aircraft and connectivity is part of its integration strategy with Delta Air Lines, aimed at attracting more business travelers.

To that end, corporate sales were up 8% in the quarter.

“Transitory inefficiencies from the sales force transformation” dented the top line, however.

The lost sales opportunities stem from the reorganization of its sales and support groups following the merger of the Air Partner and Wheels Up teams.

CEO Perspective

Mattson said, “Wheels Up made meaningful progress this quarter, completing our fleet modernization, reaching record levels of operational reliability, strengthening our Delta partnership, and building momentum with our Signature Membership.”

He added, “The entire Wheels Up team is focused on delivering a great experience for our customers while also making the business more efficient, scalable, and profitable.”

Mattson noted, “With the legacy fleet transition behind us and technology investments like BrokerOS expected to drive growth in our charter business, we enter the second half of the year with increasing confidence in our ability to execute against our plan and create long-term value for shareholders.”

In a separate letter to investors, Mattson wrote:

‘Over the past two years, we have fundamentally reshaped Wheels Up as we create a strong, durable foundation for responsible growth. We have streamlined and upgraded our fleet, improved operational reliability, unified our global sales and service teams, and implemented efficiency and cost-reduction initiatives across our business. As we move through the remainder of the year, we are focused on realizing the benefits of these actions while continuing to scale our premium fleet of Phenom and Challenger aircraft, investing in the customer experience, growing our charter business as we leverage AI-based technology, deepening our Delta partnership, and maintaining cost discipline as we work toward our goal of sustained profitability and cash generation.’

The CEO added, “Since announcing our fleet modernization in late 2024, we have invested over $300 million in our premium fleet and modifications.”

In October 2024, management revealed plans to streamline its fleet.

READ: What Delta’s Q2 filings say about Wheels Up

Q2 2026 Financials

Second quarter GAAP revenues for 2026 were $182.0 million, down 4.0% year-over-year.

The $7 million drop matched revenues lost from last year’s sale of non-core services businesses.

Q1 GAAP revenues were $168.9 million. (A chart tracking the last six quarters of Wheels Up’s financials is below.)

Gross Profit increased 336% from $2.2 million to $9.6 million year-over-year.

The improvement in Gross Profit was despite $5 million of expenses related to the fleet transformation.

Adjusted Contribution was down slightly from $23.1 million to $22.5 million.

Adjusted Contribution margin improved from 12.2% in Q2 2025 to 12.4% in the most recent quarter.

The $26.2 Adjusted EBITDA loss in Q2 2026 was down 16% to $26.2 million.

Adjusted EBITDAR loss in the quarter improved 27% to negative $19.9 million from a negative $27.3 million year-over-year.

Quarterly Net Loss increased to $107.2 million, a 30% increase from $82.3 million, year-over-year.

Total Gross Bookings, which include the total value of off-fleet charter flights, were down 8% year-over-year to $241.8 million.

Wheels Up Quarterly financials (Last 6 quarters)

Source: Wheels Up

First half 2026 Gross Bookings increased from $503.9 million to $509.0 million.

GAAP Revenue dropped from $367.2 million to $350.9 million in the first six months of this year compared to 2025.

Gross Profits increased from $1.1 million to $7.6 million over the same period.

However, Adjusted Contribution dropped to $37.3 million from $45.5 million.

Wheels Up Full Year/Half-year Financials (2018 to 2026)

Source: Wheels Up

Net Loss increased from $181.6 million to $190.2 million.

Adjusted EBITDA loss was trimmed from $61.9 million to $56.7 million.

Adjusted EBITDAR also improved to a loss of $40.7 million from $52.5 million.

Wheels Up Q2 Highlights

The Russell Indexes added Wheels Up to the Russell 2000 and Russell 3000 indexes.

It closed on a $100 million term loan backed by Delta. The Atlanta-based airline owns 36% of Wheels Up.

The private jet company marked 101 days without cancellations. That exceeded full-year 2025 performance.

Completion Rate for the quarter was 99.4%, up nearly two points.

On-Time Performance (arrival within 30 minutes of the plan) was 86.8%, up by more than six points.

Both marks were the highest since reporting began in 2023.

Wheels Up also announced plans to migrate to Surf Air’s BrokerOS charter-sourcing platform.

It consolidated branding, retiring the Air Partner brand except for cargo charters. Wheels Up acquired Air Partner in April 2022 for $107 million.

A key highlight was that it completed its fleet transition to the Phenom 300 and Challenger 300 18 months ahead of schedule.

The Embraer and Bombardier aircraft are part of its strategy to attract more business flyers via Delta Air Lines corporate accounts.

The company also withdrew the King Air fleet in April.

Signature members increased 100% year-to-date.

READ: A Brief History of Airlines and Private Jet Companies

What’s Next for Wheels Up?

With NetJets pulling back from the jet card market and focusing on fractional ownership, Mattson sees opportunities.

“Increasingly, customers want premium access without the significant upfront investment, asset value risk, high fixed costs, long-term commitments, and complexity associated with whole or fractional ownership of a single aircraft type,” he says.

Delta Air Lines Integration

Mattson said to expect more integration with Delta.

He says, “The idea is that if you go on the Delta app or the Wheels Up app, you get choices across the other ecosystem.”

“Work is being done on those concepts that were part of the original vision (and they are) coming to life,” Mattson says, although there is no timeline.

Mattson also didn’t rule out enabling Wheels Up members to earn SkyMiles on their flights, something TLC Jet launched with American Airlines earlier this year.

In April, JAL Business Aviation added points-earning in the Japan Airlines Mileage Bank loyalty program as a benefit for private jet charter customers.

Qatar Executive gives flyers four Avios in its Privilege Club frequent flyer program for every dollar spent on charter flights.

Flyers with JSX, which operates public charters using private jet terminals, earn United Airlines miles.

Currently, Wheels Up members can use funds to book Delta flights and gain SkyMiles status, including the invitation-only 360 program.

“We’ve got something that appears to be resonating in the market, specifically with those customers,” Mattson says, adding, “The way we look at it, we’re not sure (earning miles is) going to drive a significant amount of customer behavior among private aviation customers.”

Off-Fleet Charter Growth

Mattson is also bullish on expanding his off-fleet charter business through the new alliance with Surf Air and its Palantir-backed charter-sourcing platform.

The CEO says:

‘We are now enabling our team with this software platform to do something that will really change, very positively change our ability to drive growth in our charter business, and to drive higher conversion rates and better service in our charter business for our customers, which is already very high.’

Mattson expects SurfOS will increase “our ability to respond much more quickly to charter requests,” adding, “And as you know, speed of response is very much linked to conversion rates.”

Wheels Up Fleet Future

Mattson says Wheels Up will add up to 15 more Phenom and Challenger aircraft to its fleet before the end of the year.

Mattson, in his letter to shareholders, wrote, “Fleet modernization has helped us achieve a 20% improvement in overall utility for the second quarter versus the prior year, underscoring the impact of higher maintenance reliability on our new premium fleets to generate improved margin performance and a higher return on assets.”

He added, “Utility on these fleets has been pressured by our intentional decision to temporarily remove aircraft from service on a rolling basis to accelerate paint, interior, and satellite Wi-Fi investments to deliver a consistent customer experience.”

He predicted, “As these aircraft are brought back into revenue service and we continue to scale with additional aircraft acquisitions, we expect utility to further improve, pushing toward a long-term annual run-rate goal of 70 hours and helping to achieve our Adjusted Contribution Margin long-term target of 30%+.”

Cost-Cutting Benefits

Wheels Up said, it “continues to implement initiatives expected to deliver approximately $70 million or more in annual cash cost savings through operational efficiencies, productivity improvements, and overhead reductions.”

The company expects the cuts it announced last year to improve financial results in the second half of the year.

The company “substantially” completed the initiatives in the second quarter of 2026 and expects to realize the benefits by the end of 2026.

Additional data from its 10-Q will be added as soon as the report is available.

text:
Major PC manufacturers HP Inc. (NYSE:HPQ) , Asus, and Acer have reportedly begun incorporating memory chips from China’s ChangXin Memory Technologies (CXMT) amid a global chip shortage.

Major PC manufacturers have qualified CXMT’s DRAM chips and begun using limited quantities in their laptops, reported Nikkei Asia on Tuesday.

CXMT chips currently have limited adoption in laptops, with only a small number of notebook models using them. The Chinese chipmaker is prioritizing production capacity for domestic customers such as Huawei, and laptops featuring CXMT chips are mainly being sold in non-U.S. markets, according to the report.

PC makers are limiting their use of CXMT chips to avoid upsetting major global memory suppliers like Micron Technology Inc. (NASDAQ:MU) , Samsung Electronics (OTC:SSNLF), and SK Hynix Inc. ADR (NASDAQ:SKHY).

“The top three memory chipmakers accounted for more than 90% of global market share… It is a seller’s market now. We dare not source too much from CXMT at this moment,” a source told the publication.

Some PC manufacturers have secured enough CPUs and are now urgently seeking additional memory supplies, making them more willing to source chips from any available supplier, including CXMT.

PC and smartphone markets have faced ongoing shortages of memory chips and CPUs since late last year, hence they are seeking alternative sources.

HP, Acer and Asus did not immediately respond to Benzinga’s request for comments.

CXMT Growth Raises Security Concerns

CXMT’s growing adoption is a major boost for the Chinese memory chip maker, though its links to alleged Chinese military ties could create sensitivity for U.S. companies. Notably, CXMT is included on the Pentagon’s 1260H list.

While CXMT denies the allegations and is not on a trade blacklist, the company’s recent Shanghai STAR Market listing has pushed its valuation above Intel Corp’s (NASDAQ:INTEL) , marking a significant milestone.

Meanwhile, bipartisan U.S. senators have urged Apple Inc. (NASDAQ:AAPL) CEO Tim Cook to avoid using memory chips from Chinese firms CXMT and YMTC, citing concerns over their alleged links to China’s military. The request comes as Apple reportedly tested CXMT’s DRAM chips for China-market devices amid a global memory chip shortage and rising component costs.
